# Week 1 - Day 2 - Fundamentals - Environment setup & your first Playwright project

By the end of this lesson you will have checked your own Node install, know what
`npm init playwright@latest` actually produces, and have opened this repo's real
`playwright.config.ts` to recognize the pieces in it.

> **No new TypeScript today.** This is npm/CLI/editor setup, not language syntax — nothing
> to primer, so there's no Day 2.1. [Day 1.2](/learn/w1/d1/p2) covered the why; this is the
> how.

> **Try it here.** Write code in the editor on the right and press Run. Your code drives a real browser, and the results appear beside it.

| | |
|---|---|
| **You'll do** | check Node · open this repo in VS Code · read its real `playwright.config.ts` |
| **You'll learn** | what `npm init playwright@latest` writes, and why you must not run it here |
| **Where it runs** | here in the editor. The cells read real files on your disk. |
| **Assumes** | nothing but a terminal |

## 1. Node.js

Playwright (and the whole npm ecosystem it sits on) needs Node installed. Check yours:

```bash
node -v
npm -v
```

If either command isn't found, install Node from https://nodejs.org (the LTS build) and
re-open your terminal.

**Expected result:** two version strings, something like `v24.21.0` and `11.19.0` — the
exact numbers will differ on your machine, and that's fine. Any Node 18+ works with current
Playwright.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

variation.prompt: Same idea, one more tool: also print the Playwright CLI's own version with `npx playwright --version` (`npx.cmd` on Windows), alongside node and npm.

blocks.text:
## 2. VS Code

Three things worth doing once, before you write any test code:

| Step | Why |
|---|---|
| **File → Open Folder**, open this repo's root | So VS Code's IntelliSense, `tsconfig.json`, and the Jupyter extension all see the right project |
| **Trust the workspace** when prompted | VS Code sandboxes an unfamiliar folder until you trust it — required before tasks/extensions run |
| Use the **integrated terminal** (`` Ctrl+` ``) | Keeps every command you run scoped to this project's folder, with the right `PATH` |

## 3. What `npm init playwright@latest` actually does

**This repo is already a set-up Playwright project** — running that command again here
would overwrite a shared config other weeks depend on, so **don't run it in this repo**.
What follows is what it produces on a **fresh, empty folder**, so you recognize the pieces
when you see them (which you will, right below, in this repo's real files).

```bash
npm init playwright@latest
```

It asks you four questions:

| Prompt | Answer for this course |
|---|---|
| TypeScript or JavaScript? | **TypeScript** |
| Name of your tests folder | default (`tests`) is fine |
| Add a GitHub Actions workflow? | **No** — not needed for this course |
| Install Playwright browsers? | **Yes** |

It then installs `@playwright/test`, downloads the Chromium/Firefox/WebKit binaries, and
writes:

```
node_modules/            # dependencies — never edit, never commit
package.json             # your project's dependency + script list
package-lock.json        # exact installed versions, for reproducible installs
playwright.config.ts     # the file Playwright reads for every run
tests/                   # example specs, to delete once you've read them
tests-examples/          # a second folder of longer demo specs
```

A fresh `playwright.config.ts` looks roughly like this:

```ts
import { defineConfig, devices } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  testDir: './tests',
  fullyParallel: true,
  reporter: 'html',
  use: {
    trace: 'on-first-retry',
  },
  projects: [
    { name: 'chromium', use: { ...devices['Desktop Chrome'] } },
    { name: 'firefox', use: { ...devices['Desktop Firefox'] } },
    { name: 'webkit', use: { ...devices['Desktop Safari'] } },
  ],
});
```

Three browsers (`projects`), one report format (`html`), tracing only kept on a retry. All of
that is exactly what Day 3 tours in more detail.

## 4. This repo's *actual* config — open it for real

This is not a fresh scaffold — it's a shared course repo, already configured, with 8 weeks of
material depending on the same config staying put. Open `playwright.config.ts` at the repo
root (not inside `week1/`) in VS Code right now and find:

- `testMatch: ["week*/**/*.spec.ts", ...]` — this is *why* a spec you write into
  `week1/generated/` gets picked up automatically, with no registration step.
- `use: { baseURL: "https://test-automation-banking.vercel.app", ... }` — every relative
  `page.goto("/")` in this course resolves against that.

You'll read the rest of this file properly in [Day 3.3](/learn/w1/d3/p3) — for today, just
confirm you can find those two lines.

**Expected result:** the `testMatch` array (mentioning `week*/**/*.spec.ts`) and the
`baseURL` line pointing at the banking app, printed straight from the file on disk.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

blocks.text:
## Best practices

- Never run `npm init playwright@latest` inside a repo that already has a config you care
  about — it can overwrite `playwright.config.ts`.
- Commit `package.json` and `package-lock.json`. Never commit `node_modules/` (it's already
  in `.gitignore`).
- Trust the workspace once, and VS Code stops asking.

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | What you see | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Ran `npm init playwright@latest` in this shared repo | Root config gets overwritten, other weeks break | Don't — this repo is already initialized |
| Didn't trust the workspace | Extensions/tasks silently don't run | File → the trust prompt, or **View → Command Palette → "Trust Workspace"** |
| Forgot `--with-deps` / skipped the browser-install prompt | `browserType.launch: Executable doesn't exist` later | Re-run `npx playwright install` |
Why does this lesson tell you NOT to run `npm init playwright@latest` in this repo?

options: Because the command only works in an empty folder and would fail
Because it can overwrite `playwright.config.ts`, and eight weeks of material depend on that shared config
Because it would reinstall the browsers you already have
checkpoint.explanation: This repo is already a set-up Playwright project. Re-scaffolding would rewrite the root config every week's specs rely on. The lesson walks through what the command produces so you recognise the pieces — in this repo's real files, rather than by running it.

blocks.text: You write a new spec into `week1/generated/`. What makes Playwright pick it up, with no registration step?

options: Any `.spec.ts` file anywhere is collected automatically
`testMatch` in the root config, which lists `week*/**/*.spec.ts`
The `tests/` folder is scanned recursively, and `week1/` sits inside it
checkpoint.explanation: `testMatch: ["week*/**/*.spec.ts", ...]` is the line doing the work — which is exactly why the lesson asks you to find it in the real file. It is also why a helper file must not carry the `.spec.ts` suffix: the same pattern would collect it and try to run it as a test.

blocks.text: Weeks later you hit `browserType.launch: Executable doesn't exist`. What most likely happened?

options: Node is too old for the installed Playwright version
The browser download was skipped at setup — `npx playwright install` fixes it
`playwright.config.ts` is missing a `projects` entry for that browser
checkpoint.explanation: Playwright drives browser binaries it downloads separately from the npm package. Answering "no" to the install prompt, or installing on a machine that never ran it, leaves the package present and the browser missing. It is the one setup mistake that surfaces much later than it is made.

blocks.text:
- Any Node 18+ is fine; the exact numbers on your machine will differ from anyone else's.
- **Never re-scaffold a repo that already has a config you care about.** This one is already set up.
- `testMatch` in the root config is why a spec written into `week*/generated/` is found without registering it anywhere.
- `baseURL` is why every `page.goto("/")` in this course resolves to the banking app.
- Commit `package.json` and `package-lock.json`; never `node_modules/`.
- The browsers are a separate download from the npm package — `npx playwright install` if they are missing.

## What's next

[Day 2.3](/learn/w1/d2/p3) looks at how a real project organizes its test folders and config —
beyond the one flat `tests/` folder a fresh scaffold gives you.

parts.title: Organizing a real project's folders and config

blocks.text:
# Week 1 - Day 2 - Implementation - Organizing a real project's folders and config

By the end of this lesson you will understand how `testDir` and folder-per-test-type
conventions turn a flat scaffold into something a whole team can navigate, and what actually
needs to be in `.gitignore` for a Playwright project.

> No new API here — "advanced" for a setup day means organizing what Day 2.2 gave you
> sensibly, not new Playwright calls.

| | |
|---|---|
| **New API** | none — "advanced" on a setup day means organising what you already have |
| **You'll learn** | how `testDir` and `testMatch` shape a project, and what belongs in `.gitignore` |
| **Builds on** | the real config you opened in [Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d2/p2) |

## The problem with the fresh scaffold

`npm init playwright@latest` gives you one `tests/` folder. That's fine for a demo, but a
real project quickly ends up with UI tests, API tests, and maybe visual/performance tests —
all needing different setup, different fixtures, sometimes different configs. Dumping
everything into one `tests/` folder makes it hard to run "just the API suite" or "just smoke
tests" without a lot of `--grep` gymnastics.

## A convention: split by test type

A common pattern (used in the source training session, and worth knowing even before you
have both kinds of tests) is separate top-level folders per testing vertical:

```
UI_test/
  login.spec.ts
  dashboard.spec.ts
API_test/
  bookings.spec.ts
```

`testDir` in the config points at the root that contains both, and `testMatch` (or per-folder
configs, which week3/day5 covers) decides what counts as a test. This course doesn't use the
`UI_test`/`API_test` split literally — the config you read on Day 2.2 organizes by **week**
instead (`week1/`, `week2/`, …, each with its own `generated/` folder) — but the underlying
idea is the same: **group tests by what they need in common**, not by the order you wrote
them.

**Expected result:** three config shapes printed. Notice `testDir` alone isn't the whole
answer — `testMatch` is what actually decides which files count as specs once you're not
using one flat default folder.

variation.prompt: Same idea, one more shape: as plain data, write what a config would look like if it only ever ran files under a single `smoke/` folder.

blocks.text:
## `.gitignore` for a Playwright project

Three entries every Playwright project needs, and why:

| Entry | Why it's ignored |
|---|---|
| `node_modules/` | Regenerated from `package.json` by `npm install` — never source, often huge |
| `test-results/` | Per-run artifacts (screenshots, videos, traces on failure) — regenerated every run |
| `playwright-report/` | The HTML report — also regenerated every run, and would blow up repo size if committed |

This repo's real `.gitignore` has all three, plus course-specific entries (old build output,
screenshots from a legacy folder). The pattern to remember: **if a run regenerates it, it
doesn't belong in git.**

**Expected result:** `present` for all three — confirmed straight from this repo's real
`.gitignore`, not assumed.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

variation.prompt: Same file read, different entries: check the `.gitignore` for `.env` and `dist` instead of `node_modules` and `test-results`.

blocks.text:
## Best practices

- Group test folders by what they share (setup, fixtures, tags) — not by creation order.
- Keep `testDir`/`testMatch` in the config, not scattered CLI flags every run needs to repeat.
- `.gitignore` anything a run regenerates: reports, traces, screenshots, `node_modules/`.

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | What you see | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Committed `test-results/` or `playwright-report/` once | Repo size balloons, diffs are noisy binary reports | Add to `.gitignore`, then `git rm -r --cached` the committed copy |
| Two unrelated test types dumped in one folder | Can't run "just API tests" without fragile `--grep` | Split by folder, matched via `testMatch` |
You move off the flat `tests/` folder and split specs into `UI_test/` and `API_test/`. Is setting `testDir` enough?

options: Yes — `testDir` points at the root containing both, and the rest is automatic
No — `testMatch` is what decides which files count as specs once you leave the one default folder
No — each folder needs its own `playwright.config.ts`
checkpoint.explanation: `testDir` says where to start looking; `testMatch` says what counts once you are there. This repo shows the same pair in use, organised by week rather than by test type. Per-folder configs are a real option too, but they are week 3's subject, not a requirement here.

blocks.text: Which rule decides whether something belongs in `.gitignore` on a Playwright project?

options: If it is large, ignore it
If a run regenerates it, it does not belong in git
If it is not TypeScript, ignore it
checkpoint.explanation: `node_modules/` comes back from `package.json`, and `test-results/` and `playwright-report/` are rewritten every run. Committing a report once makes every later diff a pile of binary noise — and `git rm -r --cached` is then needed on top of the `.gitignore` entry.

blocks.text:
- Group test folders by what they have in common: shared setup, fixtures, tags. Do not group them by the order you wrote them.
- `testDir` finds the root; `testMatch` decides what is a spec. You usually need both.
- This course groups by week rather than by test type. The principle is the same.
- **If a run regenerates it, it does not belong in git**: `node_modules/`, `test-results/`, `playwright-report/`.

## What's next

[Day 2.4 — Practice](/learn/w1/d2/p4) checks your own setup and has you read this repo's real
config more closely. [Day 3](/learn/w1/d3/p2) covers actually *running* tests from the CLI.

# Week 1 - Day 2 - Practice - Environment setup

Three problems. The first two use your real environment and this repo's real config — no
guessing needed, everything here is something you can check.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Three problems** | your real environment, and this repo's real config |
| **Nothing to guess** | every answer is something you can read off your own machine |
| **Pulls on** | [Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d2/p2) for the config · [Implementation](/learn/w1/d2/p3) for the structure |

## When you are done

You've now got a working understanding of what this repo's config is and why it's shaped
this way. [Day 3](/learn/w1/d3/p2) is where you actually run tests from the command line.

problems.statement:
**What to build.** Print your own Node and npm versions (like Day 2.2 did), and write a
one-line comment noting them down.

**Where.** A cell in this lesson.

**How you'll know it worked.** You see two real version numbers from *your* machine, not
copied from the lesson.

**What to build.** Read this repo's real `playwright.config.ts` (like Day 2.2 did) and answer,
in comments, from what you actually see in the file — not from memory:

1. What is `baseURL` set to?
2. What does `testMatch` match?
3. Which browsers are active in `projects`, and which are commented out?

**Where.** A cell in this lesson.

**How you'll know it worked.** All three answers came from text you actually read out of the
file in this cell, not from Day 2.2's summary of it.
problems.stub:
// Problem 2 — your code here. Read the file with Deno.readTextFile like Day 2.2 did,
// or open playwright.config.ts directly in VS Code and answer in comments below.
problems.solution:
**A model answer.** Your numbers will differ — the point is that you read them out of the file rather than recalling them.

> 1. **`baseURL`** — set to the banking app, `https://test-automation-banking.vercel.app/`. It is what makes `page.goto('/')` work in a spec without repeating the host.
> 2. **`testMatch`** — the course repo widens the default so the `weekN/generated/` files are picked up. The default alone is `**/*.@(spec|test).?(c|m)[jt]s?(x)` — the `.spec.ts` rule you prove for yourself on Day 4.3.
> 3. **`projects`** — `chromium` is active; `firefox` and `webkit` are present but commented out, which is why every run so far has opened exactly one browser.

**What makes an answer good** is that all three came from text you actually opened. The habit matters more than the answers: a config you have read is a config you can change, and from Week 3 onward you change it a lot.

> This one needs the training repo on your own machine — the studio serves the lessons, not the checkout.

problems.statement:
There's no framework-shaped code yet for a true "advanced" problem today, so instead:
**if you were starting a brand-new project from scratch tomorrow** (not this shared repo),
what would you change about the fresh-scaffold config from Day 2.2? Consider: would you keep
one `tests/` folder, or split by type? Would you turn the GitHub Actions prompt on this time?
Would you keep all three browsers active from day one, or start with just Chromium the way
this repo does?

**Where.** A cell in this lesson, as comments — there's no code to run for this one.

**How you'll know it worked.** You gave a reason for each choice, not just a preference.
problems.solution:
**A model answer.** There is no single right configuration; there is a defensible one.

> **Folder layout.** I would split by type from the start — `tests/e2e/`, `tests/api/` — rather than one flat `tests/`. Renaming folders later means touching every `testMatch`, every CI job and everyone's muscle memory. Splitting on day one costs nothing.
>
> **GitHub Actions.** Yes, turn it on. The generated workflow is a reasonable starting point and a suite nobody runs on a push stops being trusted within a month.
>
> **Browsers.** Start with Chromium only. Three browsers on day one triples the runtime and, on a young suite, triples the failures you have to triage — almost none of which are real cross-browser bugs. Add Firefox and WebKit once the suite is stable.
>
> **Evidence settings.** Keep `trace: 'retain-on-failure'`. It costs nothing on a green run and is the difference between debugging a CI failure and guessing at it.

**The shape of a good answer** is a reason attached to each choice. "All three browsers because more coverage is better" is a position; "Chromium first because early failures are mostly my bugs, not browser bugs" is an argument.
